records.name: Steelman first

origin.author: Daniel Dennett (Rapoport's rules)
origin.work: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking

records.summary: Before criticising, restate the position so well its holder would wish they had said it that way, note points of agreement and what you learned. Only then attack.
records.key_question: Could the author of this idea have stated it better than I just did?
use_when: I think their argument is wrong
before I criticise this
make the strongest case for it
am I being fair to this idea
records.produces: the strongest version of the position, points of agreement and what you learned, written before any critique
records.failure_mode: Restating a weaker version and attacking that.

records.name: Red team

origin.author: Military and intelligence practice; Micah Zenko
origin.work: Red Team

records.summary: An independent group adopts the adversary's goals and tries to make the plan fail. Independence and licence to win are what make it work.
records.key_question: If I wanted this to fail, where would I attack?
use_when: red-team my plan
attack this proposal
how would a competitor beat this
find the holes in this
records.produces: a list of attacks from the adversary's point of view, ranked by damage and likelihood
records.failure_mode: A red team without independence or permission to win, which produces polite feedback.
steps: Write the plan and its goal in a few sentences.
Define the adversary: who wants this to fail, and what they can do.
Adopt the adversary's goals fully; do not defend the plan.
List every way to make the plan fail.
Rank attacks by damage and likelihood.
Hand the top attacks back to the plan's owner for answers.

records.name: Dialectical inquiry

origin.author: Richard Mason; David Schweiger et al.
origin.work: A Dialectical Approach to Strategic Planning; Group approaches for improving strategic decision making

records.summary: Build a full counter-plan resting on opposite assumptions and debate the two. Stronger than lone devil's advocacy because it forces a whole alternative to exist.
records.key_question: What plan rests on the opposite assumptions, and how well does it hold up?
records.evidence_note: Dialectical inquiry and devil's advocacy both beat consensus approaches on decision quality (Schweiger, Sandberg & Ragan 1986).
use_when: what if we're completely wrong
build the opposite case
debate this strategy properly
test our core assumptions against an alternative
records.produces: a full counter-plan built on the opposite assumptions, and the assumptions that survived the debate
records.failure_mode: A counter-plan built as a straw man so the original wins easily.
steps: List the assumptions the current plan rests on.
Negate each key assumption.
Build a complete, plausible counter-plan from the negated assumptions.
Debate the two plans assumption by assumption.
Keep the assumptions that survive and rebuild the plan on them.

records.name: Devil's advocate

origin.author: Catholic Church (advocatus diaboli)
origin.work: Canonisation procedure

records.summary: One role argues against the proposal. Effective only if the role is genuine and protected; a token advocate makes the group more confident, not less.
records.key_question: Is anyone actually arguing the other side, with licence to win?
use_when: argue against this
play devil's advocate
give me the case against
push back on my idea
records.produces: the strongest arguments against the proposal, each with what it would take to answer it
records.failure_mode: A token advocate whose objections are dismissed, which raises the group's confidence.
steps: Assign the role openly and protect it from social cost.
State the proposal as it stands.
Argue against it as strongly as possible, without hedging.
List each objection with the evidence that would answer it.
Have the group answer each objection before deciding.

records.name: Consider the opposite

origin.author: Charles Lord, Mark Lepper, Elizabeth Preston
origin.work: Considering the opposite (JPSP)

records.summary: Ask how you would evaluate the evidence if it had pointed the other way. More effective than simply being told to be unbiased.
records.key_question: Would I accept this evidence if it supported the opposite conclusion?
records.evidence_note: Consider-the-opposite reduced biased assimilation where instructions to be fair did not (Lord, Lepper & Preston 1984). Replicated in debiasing literature.
use_when: am I biased about this
the evidence supports what I already think
check my interpretation
what if the data pointed the other way
records.produces: the evidence re-read as if it had come out the other way, with the interpretation that changed
records.failure_mode: Imagining the opposite result only briefly and returning to the same reading.

records.name: Analysis of competing hypotheses

origin.author: Richards Heuer
origin.work: Psychology of Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: List every hypothesis, list the evidence, mark each piece as consistent or inconsistent with each hypothesis. Keep the hypothesis with the least evidence against it, not the most for it.
records.key_question: Which hypothesis has the least evidence against it?
use_when: which explanation fits the evidence best
several hypotheses could explain this
weigh the evidence
what's really going on
records.produces: a matrix of hypotheses against evidence with the least-contradicted hypothesis identified
records.failure_mode: Counting supporting evidence instead of looking for inconsistencies.
steps: List every plausible hypothesis, including ones you dislike.
List the significant evidence and arguments.
Mark each item as consistent, inconsistent or neutral with each hypothesis.
Drop evidence that fits all hypotheses equally; it does not discriminate.
Rank hypotheses by how much evidence is inconsistent with each.
Name what new evidence would most change the ranking.

records.name: Key assumptions check

origin.author: US intelligence community
origin.work: A Tradecraft Primer

records.summary: List every assumption the conclusion rests on, rate how well supported each is, and name what would make it false. Shows which unexamined assumption carries the most weight.
records.key_question: Which assumption, if false, brings the whole conclusion down?
use_when: what am I assuming here
check the assumptions in this plan
what has to be true for this to work
this all rests on something
records.produces: a list of assumptions rated by support, with what would make each false and the weakest load-bearing one marked
records.failure_mode: Listing only assumptions that are easy to defend.
steps: Write the conclusion or plan.
List every assumption it depends on, stated and unstated.
Rate each: well supported, partly supported, unsupported.
For each, write what would make it false.
Mark the assumptions that carry the most weight and are least supported.

records.name: Find the crux

origin.author: Center for Applied Rationality
origin.work: Double crux technique

records.summary: Find the single belief which, if it changed, would change your conclusion. Disagreement worth having is about that belief.
records.key_question: What single belief, if I changed it, would change my conclusion?
use_when: we keep arguing about this
what would change my mind
why do we disagree
find the real disagreement
records.produces: the single belief that would flip the conclusion, and what evidence would settle it
records.failure_mode: Naming a belief that would not actually change the conclusion if it flipped.
steps: State your conclusion and the other side's.
List the beliefs each conclusion depends on.
For each belief, ask: if this changed, would my conclusion change?
Keep the one belief that would flip it.
Name the evidence or test that would settle that belief.

records.name: Chesterton's fence

origin.author: G. K. Chesterton
origin.work: The Thing

records.summary: Do not remove a rule or structure until you know why it was put there. The reason may still apply.
records.key_question: Do I know why this was built before I propose removing it?
use_when: let's just get rid of this rule
this process seems pointless
why do we do it this way
remove this step
records.produces: the original reason for the rule or structure, and whether it still applies
records.failure_mode: Assuming no reason exists because none is written down.

records.name: Extraordinary claims

origin.author: Carl Sagan (after Laplace)
origin.work: Cosmos; Broca's Brain

records.summary: The evidence required scales with how much the claim contradicts what is already well established.
records.key_question: How surprising is this claim, and is the evidence proportionate?
use_when: this sounds too good to be true
is this claim credible
a surprising study says
this contradicts what we know
records.produces: the claim rated against established knowledge, with the strength of evidence it would need
records.failure_mode: Demanding extraordinary evidence for claims that are merely unfamiliar to you.

records.name: Lateral reading

origin.author: Sam Wineburg & Sarah McGrew
origin.work: Lateral Reading (Stanford History Education Group working paper)

records.summary: Judge a source by leaving it: check what other independent sources say about who is behind it, before reading it closely.
records.key_question: What do independent sources say about who produced this?
records.evidence_note: Professional fact-checkers outperformed historians and students by reading laterally (Wineburg & McGrew 2017). Training studies show gains.
use_when: is this source trustworthy
who is behind this website
can I trust this article
check this source
records.produces: a note on who is behind the source and what independent sources say about it
records.failure_mode: Reading the source closely before checking who it is, which lets its presentation persuade you.
steps: Before reading closely, leave the page.
Search for the organisation or author behind it.
Read what independent, reputable sources say about them.
Check funding, affiliations and track record.
Return to the source only if it passes.

records.name: Pre-commit update triggers

origin.author: Philip Tetlock & Dan Gardner
origin.work: Superforecasting

records.summary: Before seeing new evidence, state what result would move your estimate and by how much. Prevents re-reading any evidence as confirmation.
records.key_question: What result would make me change my mind, decided before I see it?
use_when: what would change my mind
set criteria before seeing the results
I keep reading everything as confirmation
how should this new data change my view
records.produces: a pre-registered list of results and the size of the update each would cause
records.failure_mode: Writing triggers so vague that any result can be read as meeting or missing them.

records.name: Survival score

origin.author: Panta Rhei (original)
origin.work: Panta Rhei design
origin.note: Original to Panta Rhei; describe as such.

records.summary: After the attacks, rate how much of the idea survives on a 0–10 scale, with the rule: one fatal flaw caps the score at 3, regardless of how many strengths there are.
records.key_question: After the strongest attack, how much of this is still standing?
use_when: how much of this idea survives
score this plan after the critique
is this idea still worth pursuing
how bad are these flaws
records.produces: a 0 to 10 survival score with the fatal flaw, if any, and the strongest surviving element
records.failure_mode: Averaging strengths and weaknesses so a fatal flaw is diluted.
steps: List the attacks that landed and those that did not.
Check whether any attack is fatal on its own.
If one is, cap the score at 3.
Otherwise rate from 0 to 10 how much of the idea survives.
Write the strongest surviving element and the weakest link.

records.name: Subtraction

origin.author: Gabrielle Adams, Benjamin Converse, Andrew Hales, Leidy Klotz
origin.work: People systematically overlook subtractive changes (Nature)

records.summary: People default to adding when they improve something. Explicitly ask what to remove. The subtractive option is often cheaper and better, and is missed unless prompted.
records.key_question: What could I take away instead of adding?
records.evidence_note: Eight experiments, Nature 2021: participants overlooked subtractive solutions unless cued. Robust within the paradigm; applied effect sizes unknown.
records.card: Solve it only by removing things.
use_when: this process has too many steps
we keep adding features
simplify this
what can we remove
records.produces: a list of removable parts with the effect of removing each
records.failure_mode: Removing something that carried a real function that nobody wrote down.

records.name: Kill criteria

origin.author: Annie Duke
origin.work: Quit

records.summary: Before committing, write the conditions and the date at which you will stop. Decided in advance, quitting does not depend on willpower in the moment.
records.key_question: What would have to happen, by when, for me to stop?
use_when: when should I quit
how will I know to stop
set limits on this project
I keep throwing good money after bad
records.produces: written conditions and a date at which the commitment will be stopped
records.failure_mode: Kill criteria so loose they will never trigger.
steps: Write what you are committing to.
Write the signals that would show it is not working.
Turn each signal into a measurable condition.
Set a date to check.
Tell someone who will hold you to it.

records.name: Pre-mortem

origin.author: Gary Klein
origin.work: Performing a Project Premortem (HBR)

records.summary: Imagine it is a year later and the decision failed. Write why. Imagined certainty of failure frees people to name risks they would otherwise keep quiet.
records.key_question: If this has failed a year from now, what is the most likely reason?
records.evidence_note: Prospective hindsight increased the number of reasons generated by about 30% (Mitchell, Russo & Pennington 1989). Effect on decision outcomes less studied.
use_when: what could go wrong with this
before we commit
imagine this fails
find the risks
records.produces: a list of reasons the decision failed, ranked, with a mitigation for the top ones
records.failure_mode: Writing generic risks instead of specific stories of failure.
steps: Assume it is a year later and the decision has failed badly.
Everyone writes the reasons it failed, independently.
Pool the reasons and remove duplicates.
Rank by likelihood and impact.
Add mitigations or kill criteria for the top reasons.

records.name: Weighted criteria

origin.author: Ralph Keeney & Howard Raiffa
origin.work: Decisions with Multiple Objectives

records.summary: Name the criteria, weight them before scoring, score each option, sum. The value is in the weighting conversation; the total is only as good as the weights.
records.key_question: Did I set the weights before I saw the scores?
use_when: compare these options
score these choices
which option is best overall
decision matrix
records.produces: a scoring table with weights set before scoring, totals, and a sensitivity check on the weights
records.failure_mode: Adjusting weights after scoring until the preferred option wins.
steps: List the options.
Name the criteria that matter.
Assign weights before looking at scores.
Score each option on each criterion.
Multiply and sum.
Check whether a reasonable change in weights changes the winner.

records.name: Differential diagnosis

origin.author: Clinical medicine
origin.work: Medical diagnostic practice

records.summary: List every condition that could produce the symptoms, then order tests that discriminate between them, starting with the dangerous and the common.
records.key_question: Which test would tell my top two candidates apart?
use_when: what could be causing these symptoms
rule out possible causes
several explanations fit
which test would tell them apart
records.produces: a ranked list of candidate causes with the test that discriminates between the top ones
records.failure_mode: Ordering tests by convenience and leaving the dangerous candidate untested.
steps: List every cause that could produce the observed symptoms.
Rank by likelihood and by danger if missed.
For the top candidates, find tests that would come out differently for each.
Run the most discriminating test first, starting with dangerous and common causes.
Update the list after each result.

records.name: Fallacy sweep

origin.author: Charles L. Hamblin
origin.work: Fallacies

records.summary: Runs the argument against the fallacy canon and names each structurally invalid move: false dichotomy, begging the question, equivocation, slippery slope, ad hominem, appeal to ignorance, red herring, special pleading, no true Scotsman, moving the goalposts, post hoc.
records.key_question: Which step of this argument would still look valid if its conclusion were false — and which named fallacy is doing the work there?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the fallacy sweep test
records.produces: a written fallacy sweep finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Degenerates into label-calling: naming a fallacy without showing the move actually fails in this instance, and crying fallacy at arguments that are weak but not invalid (the fallacy fallacy).
steps: List the argument's moves in order, one line each.
Check each move against the standard fallacies: straw man, false dilemma, ad hominem, appeal to authority, slippery slope, circularity, hasty generalisation, equivocation.
For each hit, restate the move without the fallacy and see whether the conclusion still follows.

records.name: Toulmin audit

origin.author: Stephen Toulmin
origin.work: The Uses of Argument

records.summary: Dissects an argument into claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal, exposing the unstated warrant that connects evidence to conclusion and the qualifier the claim quietly dropped.
records.key_question: What is the warrant — the general rule that lets this evidence count for this claim — and what backs the warrant itself?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the toulmin audit test
records.produces: a written toulmin audit finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Becomes diagram-filling: a tidy map of a bad argument, and it cannot judge whether the grounds are true, only whether the structure is complete.
steps: Write out the claim, the grounds offered for it, and the conclusion actually drawn.
Name the warrant: the unstated rule that is supposed to carry the grounds to the claim.
Test the warrant's backing and look for the qualifier and rebuttal the argument omitted.

records.name: Critical discussion rules (pragma-dialectics)

origin.author: Frans H. van Eemeren and Rob Grootendorst
origin.work: Speech Acts in Argumentative Discussions; A Systematic Theory of Argumentation

records.summary: Scores a debate against ten rules for resolving a difference of opinion on the merits — freedom, burden of proof, standpoint, relevance, unexpressed premise, starting point, argument scheme, validity, closure, usage — treating each fallacy as a specific rule violation.
records.key_question: Which discussion rule was broken, by whom, and at which stage — and would the standpoint survive if the rule were enforced?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the critical discussion rules test
records.produces: a written critical discussion rules (pragma-dialectics) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Proceduralism: winning on rule violations while the substantive evidence goes unexamined, and the ideal model fits real, messy, power-asymmetric disputes badly.
steps: Identify the stage the discussion is actually in: confrontation, opening, argumentation or conclusion.
Check the pragma-dialectical rules: no blocking the other side's standpoint, burden of proof on whoever advances a claim, no attacking a standpoint the other side does not hold.
Name each rule breach as a fallacy with its discussion cost, not as a debating foul.

records.name: Argument mapping

origin.author: Tim van Gelder (Austhink)
origin.work: Enhancing Deliberation Through Computer-Supported Argument Mapping

records.summary: Draws the argument as a tree of contention, reasons, objections and rebuttals so that unsupported premises, single-strand dependence and missing objections become visible at a glance.
records.key_question: If every box in this map had to carry its own evidence, which boxes would be empty — and does the whole conclusion hang on one strand?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the argument mapping test
records.produces: a written argument mapping finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The map inherits the mapper's reading: a contested interpretation gets frozen into boxes, and visual completeness is mistaken for soundness.
steps: Break the text into single claims, one per box.
Draw the support and objection arrows between them; mark anything asserted without support.
Attack the load-bearing boxes: the ones whose failure collapses the most downstream claims.

records.name: Socratic elenchus

origin.author: Socrates, as recorded by Plato
origin.work: Plato's early dialogues (Euthyphro, Apology)

records.summary: Tests a definition or claim by drawing out its owner's own admissions, then producing a case the owner accepts that contradicts the definition, forcing revision rather than rebuttal from outside.
records.key_question: By your own admissions, does this case count — and if it does, does your definition survive it?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the socratic elenchus test
records.produces: a written socratic elenchus finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Purely destructive: it refutes without building, can humiliate rather than persuade, and only works on claims stated as definitions or universals.
steps: Get the claim stated as a definition or a universal rule.
Draw out two or three consequences the claimant also accepts.
Show where the consequences contradict the original claim, and let the claimant revise it.

records.name: Stasis check

origin.author: Hermagoras of Temnos (transmitted by Cicero and Quintilian)
origin.work: Stasis doctrine, in Cicero's De Inventione and Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria

records.summary: Locates the actual point of dispute among four stases — fact (did it happen?), definition (what is it?), quality (how good or serious is it?) and procedure (is this the right forum or process?) — and flags parties arguing at different stases past each other.
records.key_question: Which question are we actually disputing — fact, definition, quality or procedure — and is the other side answering a different one?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the stasis check test
records.produces: a written stasis check finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Taxonomy for its own sake: real disputes often sit at several stases at once, and naming the stasis does not settle it.
steps: Ask which of the four stases the dispute is really at: fact, definition, quality, or procedure/jurisdiction.
Check whether the two sides are arguing at different stases and talking past each other.
Restart the argument at the lowest unsettled stasis; everything above it is premature.

records.name: Scholastic disputation

origin.author: Medieval universities; Thomas Aquinas (exemplar)
origin.work: The quaestio format of the Summa Theologiae

records.summary: Structures an attack as objections stated in their strongest form, in order, followed by the reply, followed by a point-by-point answer to each objection — nothing objected is left unanswered and nothing answered was not first stated fairly.
records.key_question: What are the strongest objections to this position, stated as their holders would state them — and does the position answer every one?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the scholastic disputation test
records.produces: a written scholastic disputation finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Ritual completeness: weak objections are padded in to be knocked down, and the form can simulate thoroughness while the one fatal objection is quietly omitted.
steps: State the question and the strongest objections to your own position, in the opponents' best form.
Give the contrary authority or principle (sed contra) in one line.
Answer the question, then reply to each objection in turn, conceding what must be conceded.

records.name: Principle of charity

origin.author: Neil L. Wilson; developed by W. V. O. Quine and Donald Davidson
origin.work: Substances without Substrata (Review of Metaphysics); Davidson, On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme

records.summary: Before judging an ambiguous claim, fixes its interpretation as the version that makes the speaker most reasonable and most of their statements true — charity settles what was claimed; evaluation comes after.
records.key_question: Is there a reading of this claim under which it is sensible — and are we attacking the claim, or our least charitable translation of it?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the principle of charity test
records.produces: a written principle of charity finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Over-charity: the claim is improved past anything its author meant or could defend, and the red team ends up refuting its own invention.

records.name: Rogerian restatement

origin.author: Carl Rogers; Richard Young, Alton Becker and Kenneth Pike
origin.work: Communication: Its Blocking and Its Facilitation (1951); Rhetoric: Discovery and Change (1970)

records.summary: Requires restating the other side's position to their satisfaction and delineating where it is valid before stating one's own, reducing the threat response that blocks any revision of view.
records.key_question: Can we state their position so that they say 'yes, that is what I think' — and can we name the conditions under which they are right?
use_when: about to commit to this
stress-test this choice before it is final
run the rogerian restatement test
records.produces: a written rogerian restatement finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Mistaken for agreement: restatement without a following position becomes capitulation, and with a bad-faith counterpart it buys nothing.
steps: Restate the other side's position until they confirm you have it right.
State the contexts in which their position is valid, in their terms.
Only then present your position, framed as completing theirs where the contexts differ.

records.name: Ideological Turing test

origin.author: Bryan Caplan
origin.work: The Ideological Turing Test (EconLog)

records.summary: Tests claimed understanding of an opposing view by requiring a statement of it good enough that its actual holders cannot distinguish it from one of their own.
records.key_question: Could a holder of the opposing view read our statement of it and take it for their own — and if not, what exactly did we get wrong?
use_when: attacking a consensus
check this consensus before relying on it
run the ideological turing test test
records.produces: a written ideological turing test finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Tests mimicry, not truth: passing proves understanding of a position, not that the position (or our rejection of it) is correct.
steps: Write the opposing position's case as a sincere believer would write it, first person.
Check it against real believers' texts for tells: caricature, wrong priorities, missing insider concerns.
If the imitation fails, the disagreement is not yet understood well enough to attack.

records.name: Bayesian updating

origin.author: Thomas Bayes; Pierre-Simon Laplace
origin.work: An Essay Towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances

records.summary: Forces every piece of evidence to be weighed as a likelihood ratio — how much more expected is this observation if the claim is true than if it is false — applied to a stated prior, so weak and non-diagnostic evidence stops moving beliefs.
records.key_question: What was the prior, and would we expect to see this evidence anyway if the claim were false — if so, by how much should it actually move us?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the bayesian updating test
records.produces: a written bayesian updating finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: False precision: priors and likelihoods are often guesses dressed as numbers, and the arithmetic lends spurious authority to the inputs.
steps: State the prior: how likely was this claim before this evidence arrived?
Ask the diagnostic question: how likely is this evidence if the claim is false?
Move the probability by the ratio, not by the headline; write down the new number or range.

records.name: Inference to the best explanation

origin.author: Gilbert Harman (term); Charles Sanders Peirce (abduction)
origin.work: The Inference to the Best Explanation (Review of Metaphysics)

records.summary: Ranks rival explanations of the same evidence by explanatory virtues — scope, simplicity, fit with background knowledge, fruitfulness, and how little they must add ad hoc — instead of merely listing hypotheses.
records.key_question: Of the live explanations, which explains the most with the fewest additions — and what does the favoured one leave unexplained?
use_when: which explanation actually fits
several stories could explain this
run the inference to the best explanation test
records.produces: a written inference to the best explanation finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The best of a bad lot: the loveliest explanation can still be false, and 'best' quietly slides from most likely to most satisfying.
steps: List the live explanations of the evidence, including the dull ones.
Score each on scope, fit with what else is known, and how much it has to invent.
Keep the best explanation as a working hypothesis and name the observation that would dethrone it.

records.name: Severe testing (Popper beyond falsification)

origin.author: Karl Popper
origin.work: The Logic of Scientific Discovery; Conjectures and Refutations

records.summary: Credits a claim only for surviving tests it would probably have failed if false — risky predictions and severe probes count; confirmations the claim would produce anyway count for almost nothing.
records.key_question: What test has this claim passed that it would likely have failed if it were wrong — and which of its 'confirmations' were guaranteed either way?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the severe testing test
records.produces: a written severe testing (popper beyond falsification) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Severity is judged against background knowledge, which is itself contestable; and some true claims (historical, singular) cannot be put to repeatable severe tests.
steps: Ask what test this claim has passed that it would probably have failed if it were wrong.
Discount confirmations the claim's defenders went looking for; credit predictions made in advance.
If no severe test exists, grade the claim as untested, however often it has been repeated.

records.name: Paradigm and anomaly audit (Kuhn)

origin.author: Thomas S. Kuhn
origin.work: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions

records.summary: Asks whether a field's reigning framework is quietly accumulating anomalies it reclassifies as puzzles or noise, and whether the evidence for the consensus was gathered with instruments and categories the paradigm itself supplied.
records.key_question: What observations does this field treat as anomalies or non-results — and would the consensus look as solid from outside its own categories?
use_when: attacking a consensus
check this consensus before relying on it
run the paradigm and anomaly audit test
records.produces: a written paradigm and anomaly audit (kuhn) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Over-firing: most anomaly piles are just unsolved normal science, and the audit can make every stable field look like a pre-revolutionary crisis.
steps: Name the paradigm's core commitments and what it treats as a solved problem.
List the anomalies it currently explains away, files as noise, or postpones.
Judge whether anomaly-handling is still productive or has become defensive patchwork.

records.name: Progressive or degenerating programme (Lakatos)

origin.author: Imre Lakatos
origin.work: Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes

records.summary: Judges a theory or strategy by its trajectory: progressive if its adjustments predict novel facts, degenerating if each fix only patches the latest failure after the fact while the hard core is protected by an ever-thicker belt of excuses.
records.key_question: What has this theory or strategy predicted before the fact lately — and are its recent changes discoveries, or patches applied after each failure?
use_when: which explanation actually fits
several stories could explain this
run the progressive or degenerating programme test
records.produces: a written progressive or degenerating programme (lakatos) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Hindsight-dependent: programmes can look degenerating for years and then pay off, so the audit counsels patience as often as abandonment and gives no clean stopping rule.
steps: Separate the programme's hard core from its protective belt of adjustable assumptions.
Check the recent record: do belt changes predict new facts, or only absorb failures after the fact?
A programme whose changes only absorb failures is degenerating, whatever its pedigree.

records.name: Fixation of belief audit (Peirce)

origin.author: Charles Sanders Peirce
origin.work: The Fixation of Belief (Popular Science Monthly)

records.summary: Classifies how a belief was actually settled — by tenacity (refusing to reconsider), authority (an institution decreed it), the a priori method (it is agreeable to reason or fashion), or inquiry — and discounts beliefs held by the first three.
records.key_question: How was this belief actually settled — by inquiry, or by tenacity, authority or fashion — and what would its holders do if it were challenged?
use_when: attacking a consensus
check this consensus before relying on it
run the fixation of belief audit test
records.produces: a written fixation of belief audit (peirce) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Genetic fallacy risk: a belief adopted by authority or tenacity can still be true; the audit impeaches the holding, not the proposition.

records.name: Mill's collision test (dead dogma)

origin.author: John Stuart Mill
origin.work: On Liberty, chapter 2

records.summary: Holds that a belief never exposed to its strongest opposition decays into dead dogma held as prejudice — so the audit asks when the view last faced a competent opponent, and whether its holders can state the opposing case and why it fails.
records.key_question: When did this view last collide with the strongest case against it — and can its holders state that case, and the grounds on which it is rejected?
use_when: attacking a consensus
check this consensus before relying on it
run the mill's collision test test
records.produces: a written mill's collision test (dead dogma) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Both-sides drift: collision is owed to competent opposition, not to every fringe claim, and the test says nothing about which side wins the collision.
steps: State the strongest living objection to the belief, not the weakest historical one.
Check whether believers can say why the objection fails, or only that it is held by the wrong people.
A belief nobody can defend against its best objection is a dead dogma, held as prejudice.

records.name: Cartesian rules audit

origin.author: Rene Descartes
origin.work: Discourse on the Method; Rules for the Direction of the Mind

records.summary: Applies Descartes' four precepts as an audit: accept nothing not clearly known, divide each difficulty into parts, proceed from the simplest to the most complex, and make enumerations so complete that nothing is omitted.
records.key_question: Which parts of this case were accepted without clear evidence, never divided into parts, or left out of the enumeration altogether?
use_when: attack this plan before reality does
a plan that has never been challenged
run the cartesian rules audit test
records.produces: a written cartesian rules audit finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Demands a certainty most real decisions cannot reach; applied rigidly it produces paralysis and false confidence in whatever survived introspection.
steps: Check the four rules in order: was anything accepted without clear evidence?
Was the problem divided into parts small enough to judge?
Was the reasoning ordered from simple to complex, and was the enumeration complete enough to catch omissions?

records.name: Baloney detection kit (full)

origin.author: Carl Sagan
origin.work: The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark, ch. 12

records.summary: Runs Sagan's full nine-tool kit: independent confirmation of facts, substantive debate on all sides, no reliance on chains of authority, spin multiple hypotheses, try hardest to falsify your own hypothesis, quantify, check every link of the argument chain, Occam's razor, and.
records.key_question: Is there independent confirmation, has every link been checked, and have we tried as hard to falsify our own hypothesis as the other side's?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the baloney detection kit test
records.produces: a written baloney detection kit (full) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Checklist theatre: the kit is run ceremonially over a claim already decided, and several tools (Occam, falsifiability) can be gamed by how the claim is framed.
steps: Run Sagan's kit: seek independent confirmation, look for the strongest opposing case, check the proposer's track record and incentives.
Watch for the kit's named traps: ad hominem, appeal to authority, argument from adverse consequence, straw man, suppressed evidence.
Grade the claim by how many kit tests it passes unprompted, not by how it feels.

records.name: Feynman's first principle (self-deception audit)

origin.author: Richard Feynman
origin.work: Cargo Cult Science (Caltech commencement address)

records.summary: Applies the principle that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool — by demanding the claimant report everything that could make their result wrong, including the evidence and failed runs they would rather omit.
records.key_question: What has the claimant not told us that they know — the failed attempts, the contrary data, the conditions under which this does not work?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the feynman's first principle test
records.produces: a written feynman's first principle (self-deception audit) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Unfalsifiable suspicion: absence of reported weaknesses can reflect a genuinely strong result, and the audit can slide into accusing honest reporters of concealment.

records.name: Mertonian norms audit (CUDOS)

origin.author: Robert K. Merton
origin.work: The Normative Structure of Science

records.summary: Audits the conditions a claim was produced under against science's institutional norms — communalism, universalism, disinterestedness, organised scepticism — flagging secret data, status-based judgement, undisclosed stakes and immunity from criticism.
records.key_question: Was this produced under disinterested, organised scepticism — or in secret, by interested parties, judged by who they are rather than what they showed?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the mertonian norms audit test
records.produces: a written mertonian norms audit (cudos) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Idealisation: real science routinely violates the norms and still produces truth, and norm violations impeach the process without settling the claim.

records.name: Historical source criticism (provenance audit)

origin.author: Charles-Victor Langlois and Charles Seignobos
origin.work: Introduction to the Study of History

records.summary: Subjects a document or dataset to external criticism before content is weighed — authenticity, date, authorship, chain of transmission — then internal criticism: what the author could have known, and what interest shaped the record.
records.key_question: Before what it says: what is this source, when and by whom was it actually made, how did it reach us — and what did its maker know and want?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the historical source criticism test
records.produces: a written historical source criticism (provenance audit) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Provenance perfectionism: authentic sources lie and late, copied sources can preserve truth, so a failed pedigree impeaches but does not refute.
steps: External criticism first: is the document what it claims to be — author, date, provenance, chain of custody?
Internal criticism next: what did the author intend, what could they actually know, what did they gain?
Only then use the content, discounted by everything the first two steps found.

records.name: SIFT check

origin.author: Mike Caulfield
origin.work: SIFT (The Four Moves), Hapgood

records.summary: Runs four fast moves on an online claim: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims, quotes and media back to their original context — the trace move catches the clipped quote and the recycled statistic that lateral reading alone misses.
records.key_question: Have we traced this claim, quote or figure back to its original context — and does it still say the same thing there?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the sift check test
records.produces: a written sift check finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Speed over depth: SIFT settles whether something is worth trusting at a glance, not whether it is true, and 'better coverage' can converge on the same single upstream source.
steps: Stop: do not share or rely on the claim yet.
Investigate the source: who is behind it, in thirty seconds of lateral checking.
Find better coverage and trace the claim, quote or figure back to its original context.

records.name: Propaganda device sweep

origin.author: Institute for Propaganda Analysis (Clyde R. Miller et al.)
origin.work: How to Detect Propaganda (Propaganda Analysis, vol. 1 no. 2)

records.summary: Sweeps a pitch or campaign for the seven devices: name-calling, glittering generalities, transfer, testimonial, plain folks, card stacking and bandwagon — persuasion carried by labels, virtue words and stacked selection instead of evidence.
records.key_question: Strip the labels, virtue words, endorsements and selected facts: what evidence remains once the seven devices are removed?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the propaganda device sweep test
records.produces: a written propaganda device sweep finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Device-spotting becomes the conclusion: a message can use testimonials and virtue words and still be right, and the sweep detects technique, not falsehood.
steps: Sweep the text for the seven devices: name-calling, glittering generalities, transfer, testimonial, plain folks, card stacking, bandwagon.
For each hit, rewrite the sentence with the device removed and see what evidence remains.
Judge the claim on the residue, not on the framing.

records.name: Actively open-minded thinking audit

origin.author: Jonathan Baron
origin.work: Rationality and Intelligence; Thinking and Deciding

records.summary: Scores the thinking itself against AOT standards: possibilities, evidence and goals searched thoroughly and fairly, with counter-evidence sought as hard as confirming evidence and weighed without myside discount — insufficient or one-sided search fails the audit regardless of.
records.key_question: Was the search fair — were alternatives and counter-evidence looked for as hard as confirmations, and weighed by the same standard when found?
use_when: about to commit to this
stress-test this choice before it is final
run the actively open-minded thinking audit test
records.produces: a written actively open-minded thinking audit finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Search can always be extended, so the audit needs a stopping judgement it cannot itself supply; and fair searchers can still reach wrong conclusions.

records.name: Intellectual humility audit

origin.author: Linda Zagzebski
origin.work: Virtues of the Mind

records.summary: Audits the knower rather than the claim: whether confidence tracks actual competence and evidence, limits are owned, and the arguer shows the intellectual virtues (humility, courage, carefulness) rather than the vices (arrogance, vanity, closed-mindedness) that predict.
records.key_question: Does this person's confidence match their competence and evidence — and do they behave like someone who could discover they are wrong?
use_when: attacking a judgment of a person
check this judgment of a person before relying on it
run the intellectual humility audit test
records.produces: a written intellectual humility audit finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Slides into character judgement and ad hominem: a humble person can be wrong and an arrogant one right, so the audit may only discount testimony, never refute a claim.

records.name: Quality of Information Check

origin.author: Central Intelligence Agency
origin.work: A Tradecraft Primer: Structured Analytic Techniques for Improving Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Grades each load-bearing source for reliability, completeness and independence before the argument built on it is trusted.
records.key_question: If your single weakest source is wrong, which of your conclusions falls with it?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the quality of information check test
records.produces: a written quality of information check finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Degrades into ritual grading — reliability codes assigned by gut feel, so the check certifies the evidence instead of testing it.
steps: Grade each key source: access, reliability history, and whether it reports or repeats.
Separate what is directly observed from what is inferred, assumed or passed along.
Downgrade any conclusion resting on single-source, circular or stale reporting.

records.name: Estimative language check (Kent's yardstick)

origin.author: Sherman Kent
origin.work: Words of Estimative Probability, Studies in Intelligence

records.summary: Forces every probability word in a claim ('likely', 'serious possibility') onto an agreed numerical range, exposing how much of the apparent agreement is just vague language.
records.key_question: What number, out of 100, do you actually mean by 'likely' — and would your reader pick the same number?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the estimative language check test
records.produces: a written estimative language check (kent's yardstick) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: False precision: numbers imply a calibration the analyst does not have, and the yardstick becomes decoration on the same guess.
steps: Find every probability word in the claim: likely, probably, almost certain, unlikely.
Force each onto Kent's yardstick as a number or range, and check the speaker accepts the number.
Flag any conclusion whose confidence word and evidence strength point in different directions.

records.name: ICD 203 tradecraft standards audit

origin.author: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
origin.work: Intelligence Community Directive 203: Analytic Standards (issued 2007, revalidated 2015)

records.summary: Scores an argument against nine fixed standards: sourcing, expressed uncertainty, separation of information from assumption and judgment, analysis of alternatives, relevance, logical argumentation, consistency with prior judgments, accuracy, and effective visuals.
records.key_question: Can a reader tell, at every step, what is reported fact, what is your assumption, and what is your judgment — and how sure you are?
use_when: is this claim credible
someone is asserting this as established fact
run the icd 203 tradecraft standards audit test
records.produces: a written icd 203 tradecraft standards audit finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Box-ticking: the product is edited until it looks compliant while the underlying reasoning stays untouched.
steps: Check the claim separates what is known, what is assumed and what is judged.
Check sourcing is described well enough for a reader to weigh it, and uncertainty is expressed, not buried.
Check alternatives were considered and the reasoning does not leap past its evidence.

records.name: Linchpin analysis

origin.author: Douglas MacEachin
origin.work: Foreword to Richards J. Heuer Jr., Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence)

records.summary: Identifies the few drivers of the outcome and the linchpin premises about those drivers that hold the whole conclusion up, then concentrates the attack — and the warning indicators — on those premises alone.
records.key_question: Which two or three premises, if they gave way, would bring the entire conclusion down with them?
use_when: attacking a claim / decision
check this claim / decision before relying on it
run the linchpin analysis test
records.produces: a written linchpin analysis finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The analyst picks linchpins that are easy to defend and misses the real driver, so the argument is stress-tested everywhere except where it can break.
steps: List the assumptions the conclusion rests on, then find the few about the key drivers: the linchpins.
For each linchpin ask how much would have to change for it to fail, and how we would know.
Concentrate the attack and the monitoring on the linchpins; the rest is decoration.

records.name: Mirror imaging check

origin.author: Urie Bronfenbrenner
origin.work: The Mirror Image in Soviet-American Relations: A Social Psychologist's Report, Journal of Social Issues

records.summary: Tests whether a judgment about another actor simply projects our own values, cost calculus and decision style onto them, so that their behaviour is 'predicted' by asking what we would do.
records.key_question: Are you forecasting what they will do, or what you would do in their chair?
use_when: attacking a judgment of a person
check this judgment of a person before relying on it
run the mirror imaging check test
records.produces: a written mirror imaging check finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Overcorrection: assuming the other side is wholly alien, and missing the constraints and incentives we genuinely do share.
steps: Write down how we expect the other side to reason and what we assume they value.
Check each expectation for projection: is it their logic, or ours in their clothes?
Rebuild the expectation from their history, constraints and stated doctrine.

records.name: Red Hat Analysis

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Rebuilds the situation entirely inside the other actor's worldview — their history, fears, domestic pressures and information — and re-reads their behaviour from in there.
records.key_question: Seen through their eyes, with their constraints, what does their last move actually look like it was for?
use_when: judgment of a person / explanation
run the red hat analysis test
records.produces: a written red hat analysis finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The 'other view' is a costume on our own reasoning — a caricature assembled from our stereotypes rather than their record.
steps: Adopt the adversary's or partner's worldview in first person: their history, fears, incentives and information.
From inside it, describe our plan as they will read it, not as we intend it.
Name the responses their worldview makes rational that ours calls irrational.

records.name: Red Cell analysis

origin.author: Central Intelligence Agency (Red Cell unit); Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: A small cell adopts the adversary's identity outright and plans as them — not attacking our plan from outside, but generating the move the adversary would actually make against it.
records.key_question: If you were them, tasked with defeating this plan, what exactly would you do first?
use_when: attack this plan before reality does
a plan that has never been challenged
run the red cell analysis test
records.produces: a written red cell analysis finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Threat inflation: an imaginative cell invents a cleverer, more malign adversary than the evidence supports — the Team B failure in miniature.
steps: Form the cell: a small group briefed only with what the adversary could plausibly know and do.
Have the cell plan against our proposal under the adversary's real constraints and permissions.
Take back the cell's most damaging feasible move and test the plan against it.

records.name: Team A / Team B competitive analysis

origin.author: Central Intelligence Agency (Team B chaired by Richard Pipes)
origin.work: Team B competitive analysis exercise on Soviet strategic objectives

records.summary: Two independent teams work the same evidence to rival conclusions and defend them against each other, so the disagreement itself — not one team's blind spots — becomes the product.
records.key_question: Given exactly this evidence, what is the strongest opposite conclusion a competent team could reach and defend?
use_when: attacking a consensus / claim
check this consensus / claim before relying on it
run the team a / team b competitive analysis test
records.produces: a written team a / team b competitive analysis finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: A stacked Team B: if the rival team is chosen for its conclusions, competitive analysis becomes theatre that manufactures the answer it was convened to find.
steps: Brief two teams on the same evidence with opposite mandated conclusions.
Have each build its strongest case and then attack the other's reading of the shared evidence.
Judge which case survives contact with the other, and what evidence would settle it.

records.name: Indicators and signposts (Indicators Validator)

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Converts each rival hypothesis into a list of observable indicators that should appear if it is true, then validates the list — would we actually see it, in time, and could it be faked?
records.key_question: What specific, observable events would tell you this hypothesis is the one unfolding — and are you watching for them?
use_when: attacking a plan / explanation
check this plan / explanation before relying on it
run the indicators and signposts test
records.produces: a written indicators and signposts (indicators validator) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The indicator list becomes self-confirming: analysts watch for what they listed, notice what they watch for, and read its appearance as proof.
steps: For each live hypothesis, list observable indicators that would appear if it were true.
Date and source each indicator in advance, so later sightings can be checked against the list.
Review on schedule: score which hypotheses the arriving indicators actually support.

records.name: What If? Analysis

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Assumes the unlikely or dismissed event has already happened and works backwards to build the most plausible chain by which it occurred, attacking the reasoning that ruled it out.
records.key_question: It happened. Now explain, step by step, how — and which of your 'that can't happen' arguments just failed?
use_when: attacking a plan / decision
check this plan / decision before relying on it
run the what if? analysis test
records.produces: a written what if? analysis finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Unbounded speculation: with ingenuity any outcome can be back-chained, so the exercise proves everything is possible and prioritises nothing.
steps: Take the outcome the plan assumes will not happen and stipulate it has happened.
Reconstruct, step by step, the most plausible path from today to that outcome.
Check the path for steps the current plan leaves wide open, and price closing them.

records.name: High Impact / Low Probability Analysis

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Isolates the low-probability, high-impact branch a plan has quietly priced at zero and forces it to be argued on its merits — drivers, indicators, and consequences — rather than dismissed by its odds.
records.key_question: Which outcome have you treated as negligible purely because it is unlikely, and what does the plan look like on the day it happens?
use_when: attacking a plan / decision
check this plan / decision before relying on it
run the high impact / low probability analysis test
records.produces: a written high impact / low probability analysis finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Vividness capture: a well-told catastrophe starts to feel probable, and resources chase the dramatic tail while the mundane risks go unguarded.
steps: Name the low-probability event whose impact would break the plan outright.
Test the probability honestly: is it low, or merely unexamined and uncomfortable?
Decide in advance what hedge, tripwire or exit the impact justifies, before it feels urgent.

records.name: Outside-In Thinking

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Deliberately starts from the broad external forces — demographic, technological, economic, cultural — that the inside view treats as fixed scenery, and asks which of them could overturn the argument from outside.
records.key_question: What is changing out in the world, beyond this problem's usual frame, that could make the whole argument irrelevant?
use_when: attacking a plan / consensus
check this plan / consensus before relying on it
run the outside-in thinking test
records.produces: a written outside-in thinking finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Trend soup: the external forces are so broad they can be enlisted to support any conclusion, and the analysis explains everything and predicts nothing.
steps: List the external forces the plan does not control: markets, regulators, rivals, demography, technology.
For each, describe the plausible shift that would matter most to this plan.
Bring the two or three worst shifts back inside and re-run the plan against them.

records.name: Multiple Scenario Generation

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Builds several internally consistent futures from the key drivers and their uncertainties, then tests the claim or plan against all of them instead of the single expected future.
records.key_question: In which of these futures does your argument stop working — and did you quietly plan for only one of them?
use_when: attacking a plan / decision
check this plan / decision before relying on it
run the multiple scenario generation test
records.produces: a written multiple scenario generation finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The scenario set is reverse-engineered around the preferred future: one 'expected' scenario gets the detail, the rest get the labels.
steps: Fix the focal question and the two uncertainties that matter most and are least predictable.
Build a small set of distinct scenarios from their combinations; give each a name and a logic.
Test the plan in every scenario; keep only what survives all of them or fails knowingly in one.

records.name: Cross-Impact Matrix

origin.author: Theodore J. Gordon & Olaf Helmer
origin.work: Cross-impact analysis, RAND Corporation (codified in Heuer & Pherson, 2010)

records.summary: Maps how the occurrence of each key event or trend raises or lowers the probability of every other, exposing combinations whose joint effect the argument never considered.
records.key_question: Which two things in your argument are you treating as independent that would actually trigger — or cancel — each other?
use_when: attacking a plan / explanation
check this plan / explanation before relying on it
run the cross-impact matrix test
records.produces: a written cross-impact matrix finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: False precision and combinatorial sprawl: dozens of gut-feel conditional probabilities produce an output that looks computed and is not.
steps: List the key events or trends bearing on the plan down one axis and across the other.
For each pair, judge how the first changes the second's likelihood or force.
Find the high-impact nodes: the few events whose movement moves everything else.

records.name: Hypothesis generation (Multiple Hypotheses Generator)

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Forces the full set of rival explanations to be generated and written down before any testing begins, attacking Heuer's satisficing failure: seizing the first plausible story and only ever checking it.
records.key_question: How many genuinely different explanations did you write down before you started deciding which one is right?
use_when: which explanation actually fits
several stories could explain this
run the hypothesis generation test
records.produces: a written hypothesis generation (multiple hypotheses generator) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Padding: the list is filled out with straw rivals no one believes, so the favoured hypothesis 'wins' a rigged competition.
steps: Before weighing evidence, generate the full set of plausible hypotheses, including the unwelcome ones.
Include at least one hypothesis in which we are being deceived, mistaken or played.
Only then move to weighing; a hypothesis never generated can never win.

records.name: Diagnostic reasoning (diagnosticity check)

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Tests each piece of evidence for diagnosticity — whether it actually discriminates between the rival hypotheses — instead of letting evidence that is consistent with all of them pile up as 'support' for one.
records.key_question: Which of your best evidence would look exactly the same if your main rival explanation were the true one?
use_when: attacking a explanation / claim
check this explanation / claim before relying on it
run the diagnostic reasoning test
records.produces: a written diagnostic reasoning (diagnosticity check) finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Diagnosticity is itself judged through the same biases, so evidence gets rated 'diagnostic' precisely when it flatters the favoured hypothesis.
steps: For each piece of evidence ask: which hypotheses does this actually separate?
Discard evidence that fits every hypothesis equally; it feels supportive and proves nothing.
Rank hypotheses by the diagnostic evidence against them, not by volume of support.

records.name: Deception Detection

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Asks systematically whether the evidence itself may be planted: does the source have motive, opportunity and means to deceive, does the material fit their past pattern, and is it suspiciously exactly what they would want us to believe?
records.key_question: If someone wanted you to reach exactly this conclusion, is this precisely the evidence they would feed you?
use_when: attacking a claim / judgment of a person
check this claim / judgment of a person before relying on it
run the deception detection test
records.produces: a written deception detection finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Paranoia spiral: deception is unfalsifiable once entertained — every denial becomes confirmation — and the base rate (most sources are not running a deception operation) is forgotten.
steps: Ask who gains if we believe this, and what it would cost them to fake the evidence we have.
Look for the classic tells: evidence that is too complete, too convenient, or volunteered too early.
Seek one channel the suspected deceiver does not control, and check the story there.

records.name: Chronologies and Timelines

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Lays every dated event in the story on one timeline to attack the narrative's hidden errors: reversed sequence, impossible timing, missing intervals, and causes that postdate their effects.
records.key_question: Put every event on one timeline — does the cause still come before the effect, and what falls in the gaps?
use_when: which explanation actually fits
several stories could explain this
run the chronologies and timelines test
records.produces: a written chronologies and timelines finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Sequence is mistaken for causation: a clean timeline makes post hoc reasoning feel proven rather than merely possible.
steps: Lay the known events on one dated line, with sources for each date.
Look for gaps, impossible sequences and events that only make sense in a different order.
Rebuild the causal story so it fits the timeline, not the other way round.

records.name: Structured Analogies

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson
origin.work: Structured Analytic Techniques for Intelligence Analysis

records.summary: Takes the historical analogy an argument leans on ('this is Munich, 1938') and scores it dimension by dimension — similarities, differences, and whether the differences are the load-bearing ones.
records.key_question: Your analogy matches on the surface — where does it differ, and is the difference exactly the part your conclusion depends on?
use_when: attacking a explanation / claim
check this explanation / claim before relying on it
run the structured analogies test
records.produces: a written structured analogies finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: Analogy shopping continues one level down: dimensions are chosen and weighted so the favoured comparison survives its own audit.
steps: State the present case and the historical analogy being claimed for it, side by side.

records.name: Misperception audit (Jervis)

origin.author: Robert Jervis

records.name: Hedgehog audit (Tetlock)

origin.author: Philip E. Tetlock
origin.work: Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know?

records.summary: Tests an expert claim against Tetlock's twenty-year tournament finding: forecasters who organise everything around one big idea (hedgehogs) perform worse than chance-adjacent dart-throwing, while many-small-ideas foxes do measurably better — so the audit asks how much of the.

check this claim / consensus before relying on it

origin.author: Richards J. Heuer Jr. & Randolph H. Pherson

records.name: Noise audit

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony & Cass R. Sunstein

records.name: Mediating Assessments Protocol (MAP)

origin.author: Daniel Kahneman, Dan Lovallo & Olivier Sibony

Combine the scores by the agreed rule, not by a final holistic impression.

records.name: Reference class forecasting (outside view)

origin.author: Bent Flyvbjerg, building on Daniel Kahneman & Dan Lovallo
origin.work: From Nobel Prize to Project Management: Getting Risks Right (Project Management Journal); Timid Choices and Bold Forecasts (1993)

run the reference class forecasting test

records.name: Calibration training and Brier scoring

origin.author: Glenn W. Brier; Sarah Lichtenstein & Baruch Fischhoff
origin.work: Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability (1950); Training for Calibration (1980)

Show the forecaster their own track record before their next confident number is used.

records.name: Superforecasting practices (fox-style aggregation)

origin.author: Philip E. Tetlock & Dan Gardner
origin.work: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction (building on Expert Political Judgment, 2005)

records.summary: Beyond updating: use granular probabilities instead of verbal ones, break questions into parts, aggregate many small models fox-style rather than betting on one big theory, and forecast in teams that trade arguments.

origin.author: Jennifer S. Lerner & Philip E. Tetlock

records.name: Decision journal

records.name: Checklist

origin.author: Atul Gawande

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Atul Gawande, 2009); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.

origin.author: Gary Klein, Brian Moon & Robert R. Hoffman

records.name: Fermi estimation

origin.author: Enrico Fermi

origin.author: Ole Peters

Test the plan's performance in each future; mark where it breaks rather than where it shines.
Prefer the option that stays acceptable across the set over the one that is optimal in one future.

Stress the plan inside each story and keep the moves that help in several stories at once.

origin.work: The Theory of Statistical Decision, Journal of the American Statistical Association

Find each option's worst regret across states.
Prefer the option whose worst regret you can actually live with.

origin.author: Abraham Wald

records.summary: Ignore probabilities entirely and choose the option whose worst possible outcome is least bad — the guaranteed-outcome principle.

Compare options by those worst cases, not by their expected or hoped cases.
If the leading option's worst case is ruinous and another's is merely bad, the ranking flips.

origin.author: Jeff Bezos

steps: From the estimated edge and odds, compute the full Kelly fraction, then take half or less of it.
Check the stake actually proposed against that fraction; flag anything above full Kelly as growth-destroying.
Re-run with the honest, wider uncertainty: sizing shrinks fast when the edge is a guess.

records.name: Margin of safety

origin.author: Benjamin Graham
origin.work: The Intelligent Investor

records.summary: Because estimates are wrong and the future is uncooperative, only act when the case survives a substantial cushion of error — the gap between price (or commitment) and conservatively estimated value is the protection.
records.key_question: How wrong can the central estimate be before this stops working — and is that cushion bigger than our demonstrated ability to estimate?

run the margin of safety test
records.produces: a written margin of safety finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The cushion is set by feel and quietly shrinks under enthusiasm; a margin computed from the same wrong model protects nothing.

origin.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb

origin.author: Charles Goodhart
origin.work: Problems of Monetary Management: The U.K. Experience

records.summary: Any observed statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control: a measure turned into a target stops measuring what it measured.

records.name: Campbell's law

origin.author: Donald T. Campbell
origin.work: Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change

records.evidence_note: Documented in the research literature (Donald T. Campbell, 1979); apply as a discount on judgment, not as proof in a single case.
records.summary: The more a quantitative indicator is used for decision making, the more it is subject to corruption pressures and the more it corrupts the process it was meant to monitor.

records.name: Cobra effect (perverse incentive)

origin.author: Horst Siebert
origin.work: Der Kobra-Effekt
origin.note: Siebert (2001) coined the term; the Delhi cobra anecdote itself is folklore.

records.summary: A reward offered to reduce a problem can pay people to produce more of it — the bounty breeds the cobras. (The term is verified; the colonial Delhi anecdote behind it is unverified folklore — see notes.)

records.name: Opportunity cost

origin.author: Friedrich von Wieser
origin.work: Der natürliche Werth (Natural Value)

records.summary: The true cost of any choice is the best alternative it forecloses; an option that beats doing nothing can still lose to the option it displaces. (Standard attribution of the term to von Wieser.)
records.key_question: Compared with what? What is the best alternative this commits us against, and does the favourite beat that — or only beat zero?

run the opportunity cost test
records.produces: a written opportunity cost finding: where the object fails, where it holds, and how badly
records.failure_mode: The foreclosed alternative is hypothetical and easily inflated; an imaginary perfect alternative can veto every real one.

records.name: Teleology check (fictional finalism)

origin.author: Alfred Adler
origin.work: The Neurotic Character (Über den nervösen Charakter)

records.summary: People are pulled by the goal they are moving toward — a largely unconscious, self-invented 'fictional final goal' — more than they are pushed by the causes they cite; judge the proposal by what it reliably achieves, not by what it says.
records.key_question: Forget the stated reasons: what outcome does this behaviour or proposal consistently produce, and is that its real goal?

run the teleology check test
records.produces: a motive read: the goal the behaviour actually serves, stated as a hypothesis to test
records.failure_mode: Teleology can become unfalsifiable mind-reading: any outcome can be declared the 'real goal' after the fact, so the audit must predict, not just retell.
steps: Set aside the stated reasons and ask what goal the behaviour or proposal actually moves toward.
Check the movement, not the words: what will be different, for whom, if this succeeds on its own terms?
Judge the proposal by the goal its structure serves, including the goals nobody declared.

records.name: Private logic vs common sense

origin.author: Alfred Adler
origin.work: Understanding Human Nature

records.summary: Each person reasons from a private logic — self-consistent convictions about self, others and life ('I am…', 'others are…', 'therefore I must…') — that may contradict common sense, the shared logic by which the community actually runs.
records.key_question: Which premise of this argument is private logic — true only inside the arguer's own system — and would it survive being stated plainly to the people it affects?

run the private logic vs common sense test

records.failure_mode: Majority opinion is not automatically common sense; the audit can degenerate into 'everyone disagrees with you, therefore you are wrong'.

records.name: Safeguarding tendencies

origin.author: Alfred Adler
origin.work: The Neurotic Character (Über den nervösen Charakter)

records.summary: When self-esteem is threatened, people protect their inflated self-image with safeguarding manoeuvres — excuses ('yes, but…'), aggression (attacking the critic, the data or the process) and distancing (delay, vagueness, withdrawal) — rather than facing the task.
records.key_question: What would this person have to admit if they dropped the excuse, the attack or the delay — and what is the manoeuvre protecting?

run the safeguarding tendencies test
records.produces: a motive read: the goal the behaviour actually serves, stated as a hypothesis to test
records.failure_mode: Real obstacles exist: not every 'yes, but' is a defence, and labelling a legitimate objection as safeguarding is itself a way to win an argument unfairly.

records.name: Inferiority, compensation and striving for significance

origin.author: Alfred Adler
origin.work: Study of Organ Inferiority and Its Psychical Compensation

records.summary: Feelings of inferiority are universal and fuel a striving for significance; compensation is healthy when it meets the real task and distorted when it seeks superiority over others or significance without contribution.
records.key_question: What inadequacy is this plan compensating for — and does it answer the real weakness, or buy the feeling of significance instead?

records.produces: a motive read: the goal the behaviour actually serves, stated as a hypothesis to test
records.failure_mode: Compensation is easy to allege and hard to disprove; used carelessly it pathologises ordinary ambition.

records.name: Social interest test (Gemeinschaftsgefühl)

origin.author: Alfred Adler
origin.work: Understanding Human Nature

records.summary: Adler's criterion of soundness: a solution is healthy if it works on the useful side of life — solving the problem in a way that serves the community it lands in, with a felt sense of belonging and contribution.
records.key_question: Does this plan succeed only by exporting its costs onto people who are not in the room — and would it still be chosen if they were?

run the social interest test test

records.name: Style of life and early recollections

origin.author: Alfred Adler
origin.work: The Science of Living

records.summary: By early childhood each person settles a style of life — a consistent pattern of meeting every task the same way — and the stories they tell about their earliest memories reveal its guiding line better than their stated values do.
records.key_question: What is the pattern across this person's last five decisions — and does this proposal repeat it, including the part that keeps failing?

records.produces: a motive read: the goal the behaviour actually serves, stated as a hypothesis to test
records.failure_mode: Pattern-matching on a handful of anecdotes invites narrative fallacy; early recollections are projective material, not records, and must be used as hypotheses.

records.name: Three life tasks audit

origin.author: Alfred Adler
origin.work: What Life Should Mean to You

records.summary: Every solution is eventually tested against the three tasks no one can delegate or dodge — work (occupation), friendship (society and belonging) and love (intimacy) — and a plan that solves one by silently cannibalising another has not solved it.
records.key_question: Which of the three tasks does this plan feed, and which one does it quietly tax — work, people, or love?

records.failure_mode: The three tasks are a lens, not a budget: almost any cost can be redescribed as taxing some task, so the audit needs concrete, named costs to bite.

origin.author: Rudolf Dreikurs
origin.work: Children: The Challenge

records.summary: For Dreikurs, misbehaviour and giving up are discouragement, not defect: people act as well as they feel they belong and are capable — so a workable plan must supply encouragement (building the courage to act imperfectly), not just incentives, praise or penalties.

records.failure_mode: Encouragement can be confused with softness; it does not remove consequences, and some failures really are skill or resource gaps, not courage gaps.
